title: Theories and Models of Maternal and Child Health Care I
introduction: Midwifery views pregnancy and childbirth not merely as clinical deliveries but as profound developmental transitions creating both a mother and a baby. Applying structured nursing and human-needs frameworks—spanning twelve major nursing theorists, Callista Roy's Adaptation Model, Abraham Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs, and Halbert Dunn's Wellness Theory—helps nurses prioritize care and guide families toward high-level wellness.
learningOutcomes: 7.1 Summarize the core concepts and clinical care focus of twelve major nursing theorists applied in maternal and child health nursing.
7.2 Explain Sister Callista Roy's Adaptation Model, including its four adaptive modes, regulator and cognator subsystems, and focal, contextual, and residual stimuli.
7.3 Outline Abraham Maslow's five-tier Hierarchy of Human Needs, characteristics of basic needs, 14 B-values, and traits of self-actualized individuals.
7.4 Describe Halbert Dunn's Theory of basic needs, the seven characteristics of basic needs, and healthy versus unhealthy need satisfaction.
7.5 Analyze the four factors affecting need satisfaction and the clinical criteria used to prioritize competing client needs.

content.heading: Midwifery Philosophy and Overview of Twelve Major Nursing Theorists
content.body: Both midwifery and medical models prioritize maternal and neonatal safety, yet midwifery equally values childbirth as an emotionally, socially, culturally, and spiritually meaningful transition that strengthens mothers and bonds families—encompassing breastfeeding and mothercraft. Nursing theories map relationships among client, nurse, health, and environment across general system, subsystem, adaptive, personal, interpersonal, and social approaches. Twelve foundational theorists guide MCH care: (1) Patricia Benner—nursing is a caring relationship advancing from novice to expert intuition; (2) Dorothy Johnson—persons consist of balanced behavioural subsystems whose disruption demands nursing care; (3) Imogene King—action, reaction, interaction, and transaction to achieve goal attainment; (4) Madeleine Leininger—transcultural care integrating cultural healing beliefs; (5) Florence Nightingale—structuring environmental elements (ventilation, temperature, odours, noise, light) to support recovery; (6) Betty Neuman—open system reducing stressors via primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention; (7) Dorothea Orem—self-care deficit theory delivering wholly compensatory, partly compensatory, or supportive-educational care; (8) Ida Jean Orlando—interactive process in which the client defines their own needs; (9) Rosemarie Rizzo Parse—human science viewing man-living-health as a lived unit; (10) Hildegard Peplau—interpersonal process across orientation, identification, exploitation, and resolution; (11) Martha Rogers—viewing humans as constantly changing wholes optimizing environmental interaction; and (12) Sister Callista Roy—aiding client adaptation to environmental change.

content.heading: Sister Callista Roy's Adaptation Model
content.body: Propounded by Sister Callista Roy (1980), Roy's Adaptation Model views the person as a holistic adaptive system using coping mechanisms to conserve energy and preserve equilibrium across four adaptive modes: (1) Basic Physiological Needs—spanning seven areas: exercise/rest (immobility, fatigue, insomnia), nutrition (malnutrition, nausea/vomiting), elimination (retention, constipation, diarrhoea, incontinence), fluid and electrolytes (dehydration, oedema), oxygen (ischaemia, fatigue), circulation (shock, heart failure), and regulation of temperature, senses, and endocrine function (fever, hypothermia, sensory overload/deprivation); (2) Self-Concept—divided into physical (body image and sensations), personal (ethics, values, ideal behaviour), and interpersonal (perceived interaction with others); (3) Role Mastery/Function—instrumental and expressive societal positions vulnerable to role conflict or role failure; and (4) Interdependence Relations—balancing dependence and independence (failure leads to alienation, rejection, aggression, hostility, loneliness, or dominance). Coping operates via the Regulator subsystem (reacting to internal/external physical stimuli) and the Cognator subsystem (reacting to psychosocial stimuli through perception, learning, judgment, and emotion). Stimuli arise from three sources: Focal (immediate environmental changes), Contextual (other internal/external influencing factors), and Residual (relevant personal traits). The nurse's purpose is to identify stimuli causing maladaptation and alter them so the client's regulator and cognator subsystems resume effective adaptation.

content.heading: Abraham Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs and Self-Actualization
content.body: Abraham Maslow (1940, 1970) defined a basic need as a satisfaction whose absence breeds illness, presence prevents illness, restoration cures illness, is preferred under free choice when deprived, and remains functionally inactive in healthy people. Needs motivate goal-directed behaviour across five priority levels from pyramid base to apex: (1) Physiologic Needs (air, food, water, fluids, sleep, rest, exercise, sex, temperature maintenance, elimination, shelter—most critical for survival); (2) Safety and Security Needs (physical and psychological stability, law, order, predictability, protection from pain, harm, and loss); (3) Love and Belonging Needs (giving and receiving affection, companionship, group/family identification—unmet needs cause alienation); (4) Self-Esteem Needs (internal competence, independence, self-respect and external recognition, status, prestige); and (5) Self-Actualization (realizing full potential—time-competent, inner-directed, autonomous, encompassing cognitive and aesthetic pursuits). Later, Maslow (1971) contrasted deficiency needs with growth needs called 'Being values' (Metaneeds / B-values), whose deprivation causes 'metapathology' ('sickness of the soul'), listing 14 unranked B-values (truth, goodness, beauty, wholeness, uniqueness, perfection, completion/competition, justice, simplicity, richness, effortlessness, playfulness, self-sufficiency). Self-actualized individuals exhibit 18 hallmark traits including objectivity, accurate judgment, clear ethics, humility, vocation dedication, creativity, openness, integrated personality, independence, resistance to conformity, and problem-centred focus. In nursing, Maslow's framework prioritizes nursing diagnoses, fosters therapeutic rather than emotional responses, and helps clients find meaning, control, and self-respect during illness.

content.heading: Halbert Dunn's Theory and Characteristics of Basic Needs
content.body: Halbert (Helbert) Dunn proposed a set of basic needs required to attain maximum functioning or high-level wellness: survival, communication, fellowship, growth, imagination, love, environment, communication with the universe, philosophy of living, dignity, freedom, and space—with Jourard (1963) adding physical/mental health, freedom, challenge, cognitive clarity, and varied experience. At any moment, different needs assume greater relative importance. Seven universal characteristics define basic needs: (1) all people share them, though culture modifies perception; (2) people meet needs by personal priority (e.g., a mother feeding her baby before herself); (3) some needs can be deferred (e.g., completing education before marriage); (4) unmet needs produce homeostatic imbalances and illness; (5) needs arise from internal stimuli (thinking of food) or external stimuli (food aroma); (6) culturally learned experiences shape how people respond to needs; and (7) needs are interrelated (hydration depends on adequate urinary elimination). Healthy need satisfaction causes no harm to self or others, aligns with socio-cultural values, and respects the law; unhealthy behaviour violates one or more of those criteria.

content.heading: Factors Affecting Need Satisfaction and Assigning Clinical Priorities
content.body: While meeting physiological needs is judged largely objectively, psychological need satisfaction is strictly subjective—if a client feels a psychological need is unmet, it remains unmet regardless of appearances. Four major factors influence a person's ability to satisfy needs: (1) Illness (e.g., a woman post-caesarean section needs IV fluids, mobility assistance, and reassurance before advancing to higher needs); (2) Significant Relationships (family, support systems, and a trusting nurse-client relationship help identify healthy ways to meet needs); (3) Self-Concept (positive self-regard improves recognition and healthy maintenance of needs); and (4) Developmental Stage (achieving Erikson's foundational trust helps clients feel safe and transfer trust to health workers). Because human needs are dynamic, nurses and clients prioritize them continually: life-threatening physiological deficits (such as air in a suffocating client) always take first priority. When no single survival emergency dominates, nurses weigh four factors: Perceptions (a grand multipara may not perceive a need for family planning), Health status (avoiding strenuous exercise immediately after surgery), Socio-cultural background (a mother prioritizing preparing her husband's breakfast over bed rest), and Support persons (a teenager joining a gang when family belonging is absent).

inTextQuestions.question: In Dorothea Orem's self-care theory, what are the three levels of nursing care provided based on a client's ability to complete self-care?
inTextQuestions.answer: Wholly compensatory (client has no role), partly compensatory (client participates partially), and supportive-educational (client performs own care with guidance).

inTextQuestions.question: In Callista Roy's Adaptation Model, how do the regulator and cognator subsystems differ?
inTextQuestions.answer: The regulator subsystem reacts to internal and external physical stimuli, whereas the cognator subsystem reacts to internal and external psychosocial stimuli through perception, learning, judgment, and emotion.

inTextQuestions.question: According to Maslow (1971), what is 'metapathology', and what causes it?
inTextQuestions.answer: Metapathology ('sickness of the soul') occurs when an individual's higher growth needs—called Being values (Metaneeds / B-values)—are not met.

inTextQuestions.question: What distinguishes a healthy way of meeting a basic need from an unhealthy way?
inTextQuestions.answer: Healthy need satisfaction is not harmful to self or others, conforms to the individual's socio-cultural values, and stays within the law; unhealthy behaviour violates one or more of these criteria.

saqs.question: Match each of the following nursing theorists with their major concept: Florence Nightingale, Madeleine Leininger, Betty Neuman, and Imogene King.
saqs.answer: Florence Nightingale: structuring environmental elements (ventilation, temperature, odours, noise, light) to promote recovery. Madeleine Leininger: transcultural nursing focusing on cultural beliefs and caring behaviours. Betty Neuman: open system reducing stressors via primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention. Imogene King: nursing as action, reaction, interaction, and transaction helping clients achieve goal attainment.

saqs.question: Explain Callista Roy's Adaptation Model, naming its four adaptive modes and three sources of stimuli.
saqs.answer: Roy's model views the person as a holistic adaptive system maintaining equilibrium across four modes: Basic Physiological Needs (7 areas), Self-Concept (physical, personal, interpersonal), Role Mastery/Function, and Interdependence Relations. Stimuli come from three sources: Focal (immediate environmental change), Contextual (other internal/external influencing factors), and Residual (relevant personal characteristics). Nurses alter maladaptive stimuli to restore effective regulator/cognator coping.

saqs.question: List Abraham Maslow's five categories of human needs in priority order and state the five characteristics of a basic need.
saqs.answer: From base to apex: (1) Physiologic needs, (2) Safety and security needs, (3) Love and belonging needs, (4) Self-esteem needs, and (5) Self-actualization. A basic need's absence breeds illness, its presence prevents illness, its restoration cures illness, it is preferred by a deprived person under free choice, and it is functionally inactive in a healthy person.

saqs.question: Outline Halbert Dunn's Theory of high-level wellness and explain any four characteristics of basic needs.
saqs.answer: Dunn identified basic needs essential for maximum functioning/high-level wellness (including survival, communication, fellowship, growth, imagination, love, environment, communication with the universe, philosophy of living, dignity, freedom, and space) whose relative importance shifts over time. Four characteristics of basic needs: they are universal yet culturally modified, met according to personal priorities, capable of being deferred, and interrelated (plus unmet needs cause illness and they arise from internal or external stimuli).

saqs.question: Identify the four factors that affect a client's ability to satisfy basic needs and the four factors nurses consider when assigning priorities to non-emergent needs.
saqs.answer: Factors affecting need satisfaction are illness, significant relationships, self-concept, and developmental stage. When no immediate survival threat (like lack of air) dictates top priority, nurses weigh client perceptions, current health status, socio-cultural background, and support persons.
